newsitem.title: JAPAN: Abduction case delays Japan's N.Korea aid decision.
newsitem.headline: Abduction case delays Japan's N.Korea aid decision.

text.p: Japan will not give food aid to hunger-plagued North Korea until the communist country answers charges that it abducted a Japanese girl in 1977, Tokyo's foreign minister said on Monday.
"Without progress toward a resolution of those suspicions, the public will not accept a decision to go ahead with aid," Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a parliamentary security committee.
"It's not a simple matter of replying to the United Nations World Food Programme appeal," Ikeda said of the WFP's February request for $41.6 million to help Pyongyang stave off hunger.

WFP Executive Director Catherine Bertini, who visited Japan and South Korea last week, said recent inspections found the potential for starvation "on a massive scale" in North Korea with rations to the military cut and people eating tree bark.
South Korea has pledged $6 million and the United States $10 million in a response to the appeal.
Both countries hope to entice Stalinist North Korea to join in peace talks to ease tensions on the Korean peninsula.

The abduction allegations came to light in February, when Japanese media quoted South Korean security officials as saying that a North Korean defector had knowledge of a Japanese girl who was abducted 20 years ago.

The description of the girl by the North Korean defector closely resembled the case of Megumi Yokota, then 13, who went missing in 1977 on her way home from school in a coastal village in Niigata Prefecture, central Japan, the reports said.

The Japanese government, initially cautious about the accounts, had come to believe the girl had been abducted and taken to North Korea, the Asahi Shimbun quoted unnamed foreign ministry officials as saying at the weekend.
Japan has said as many as nine Japanese citizens may have been abducted by North Korean agents and taken to the communist country in the past while two others barely escaped kidnap attempts.
Reported abductions of Japanese citizens by North Korea have clouded efforts to establish diplomatic relations between the two countries.

Confessed North Korean spy Kim Hyon-hui, who plotted to blow up a Korean Airlines Boeing 707 in 1987, said another woman who went missing in 1978 taught her the Japanese language and customs so that she could escape notice on her missions.
State media in Pyongyang, which has repeatedly denied the allegations, on Saturday slammed Japan for bringing up the abduction issue.

The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said Japanese mention of the issue helped what it said was South Korea's campaign "to impair the international image (and)...impede international assistance to North Korea."
